questions.text: What is Morgan Stanley's strategy to increase their net new assets?

claims.text: On the 3Q25 earnings call (October 2025), CFO Sharon Yeshaya said NNA is "just the beginning". She described workplace and IPOs as ways to build out the integrated firm. She said the firm has people to "shepherd individuals across the entire firm", including institutional securities and underwriting. She also said there is "a lot more to go" in working with companies and their founders and serving them throughout the corporate lifecycle.

On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), management called 2025 "consistent execution of our strategy". It cited full-year net new assets of $356 billion and fee-based flows of $160 billion as demonstrating "industry-leading growth". It said Workplace and E-Trade relationships "continue to seek out advice". The 2025 10-K (published February 2026) reports the same $356 billion NNA and $160 billion fee-based flows.

The January 2026 strategic update deck presents a Wealth Management slide titled "Driving Growth and Strong Performance". It has panels headed "Attracting Net New Assets" and "Momentum in Fee-Based Flows", comparing 2016-2020 with 2021-2025. The deck's end notes define Core Client Relationships as Advisor-Led Households, Self-Directed Households and Workplace Participants, measured at 4Q 2020 and 4Q 2025.

On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), the CFO reported record NNA of $148 billion, with stock plan IPO flows just over half of it. She described Workplace as "a strong contributor to the top of the funnel" and said the "client acquisition funnel is becoming increasingly evident". She said Workplace "brings relationships and assets onto the platform" and that the firm is positioned to support them. She said the firm continues to deliver advice and solutions to new and existing relationships, "supporting the build in our fee-based assets", and that its investments are "extending our runway for growth".

She said the firm's "pipeline and our connectivity across channels" let it "build relationships early and deepen them over time". He said newer advisors are, in his words, "blown away" by the culture and technology. questions.text: What is Schwab's strategy for its RIA custody business?

claims.text: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) describes the Advisor Services segment as providing custodial, trading, banking and trust, and support services to independent RIAs, independent retirement advisors, and recordkeepers.

The 2025 10-K states that RIAs and their clients have access to Schwab's broad range of wealth services (individual securities, mutual funds, ETFs, alternative investments, fixed income, managed accounts, cash products, bank lending, trust services). As custodian, Schwab earns revenue tied to the underlying client assets, predominantly net interest revenue and asset management and administration fees, and does not charge the RIA or end client a custody fee.
The 2025 10-K describes Schwab's educational and event support for RIAs, including industry research, practice-management programs and the annual IMPACT conference.

The 2025 10-K names competitors in Advisor Services: institutional custodians, wirehouses, regional and independent broker-dealers, fintech custodians, banks, and trust companies. It says the firm's overall strategy rests on the principle that trusted relationships bring more assets from new and existing clients, which drives revenue. Management lists scale as a key competitive advantage across both segments.

On the 1Q25 earnings call (April 2025), CEO Rick Wurster said Schwab is a leader in two of the fastest-growing segments of financial services, self-directed investors and registered investment advisors. He cited being number one in RIA custodial assets.

On the 3Q25 earnings call (October 2025), Wurster said Schwab is deepening relationships with the 16,000 RIA firms it serves by building "a broader support ecosystem that extends beyond custody alone." He cited more lending support, more alternatives capability, an institutional no-transaction-fee mutual fund platform expanded to funds from nearly 60 managers, and the launch of Advisor ProDirect for breakaway advisors.

In the 2Q26 results release (July 2026), Schwab noted that long/short strategy interest remained strong among RIA clients. Margin loan debits were $42.1 billion and short cash credits were $43.7 billion as of June 30, 2026.

The 2Q26 deck (July 2026) says Schwab "remains the trusted platform of choice for investors & RIAs" and shows it ranked #1 in RIA custodial assets. On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Wurster repeated that Schwab is #1 by RIA custodial assets.
claims.source_label: SCHW deck 2026-06-30, p.8 [IR]; SCHW transcript 2026-09-30 [IR]; SCHW deck 2026-09-30, p.7 [IR]

claims.text: Trade press (WealthManagement.com, 2026-10-28, indicative only) reports Wurster told advisors at Schwab Impact that Schwab will continue to focus on custody for RIAs with under $100 million AUM. It quotes him saying Schwab's role is "to provide a platform and a support ecosystem that helps you support your clients and helps your firm thrive." The article links this to Fidelity's move to require firms under $100 million to leave its platform by June 30, 2027.

questions.text: What is Merrill's advisor growth strategy, and how has it changed?

claims.text: On the 1Q25 earnings call (April 2025), the CFO said GWIM expense growth of 9% supported technology investment and "the cost of hiring to add experienced advisors to the platform in Merrill and the private bank." This statement covers Merrill and the Private Bank together (GWIM segment).

On the 2Q25 earnings call (July 2025), the CFO said the firm "continued to add financial advisors to the sales force in Merrill and the Private Bank through our extensive training program and experienced hiring of advisors." He said approximately one-third of net new households in Q2 were added by newly trained advisors. He again cited the cost of hiring experienced advisors in Merrill and the Private Bank as an expense driver.

The GWIM Foundational Beliefs slide from the November 2025 investor day says management believes "having the best advisors enables us to deliver exceptional client outcomes". It also says growth of fully advised client relationships "drives financial outcomes".

On the 4Q25 earnings call (January 2026), the CFO said Merrill financial advisors see the value of the franchise and "we're picking up the recruiting of experienced advisors." He said that "isn't an enormous part of our strategy" and described a training program for people in wealth management, Bank of America and Merrill. He said management believes it can keep driving that program to improve net new flows.

On the 1Q26 earnings call (April 2026), the CFO said management is focused on "adviser productivity" and is "driving productivity higher on both newer and existing members of our financial advisers team." He said the firm continues "to attract talent across both new and experienced advisers."

On the 2Q26 earnings call (July 2026), the CFO said both Merrill and the Private Bank "continued to attract talented advisers who are drawn to the breadth of our platform." He said strong adviser productivity, digital engagement and new AI-enabled tools help advisers prepare for client conversations and deliver personalized advice at scale.

On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), the CFO referred to the Merrill 5% guide, aiming for 5% over the next 3 to 5 years, and said the firm is "off to a good start". He said the goal for Merrill leadership is to "just keep growing the sales force." He also said "adviser attrition is now at near historic lows" and that "we've got more to do."

On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), the CFO said Merrill added about 4,200 net new households with at least $500,000 in assets, up 17%. He said the results reflect demand for advice and "our ability to attract clients and experienced advisers to the platform." He cited advisor productivity, digital engagement and AI tools as expanding capacity to deliver personalized advice at scale.

A Merrill press release (15 September 2026) announced the Tax Efficient Transition Service and Dollar Cost Averaging Service. The head of Managed Account Advisors at Merrill said they reflect "a continued focus on making it easier for advisors to implement personalized investment strategies at scale."

Merrill's advisor recruiting pages (page content as of 2026-11-03) pitch experienced advisors on the brand and on infrastructure supporting lead generation through Bank of America's bank and trust division. They also pitch access to Merrill's wealth management platform and Bank of America's banking and trust capabilities. questions.text: Where is Morgan Stanley investing in technology for its advisors?

claims.text: On the 1Q25 earnings call (April 2025), CEO Ted Pick said the financial advisor sees the integrated firm offering "unique access to intellectual capital, world-class technology, compensation that is viewed to be fair and motivating." This is general positioning, not a named advisor tool.

On the 3Q25 earnings call (October 2025), CFO Sharon Yeshaya named early AI use cases, some live and some in pilot. The advisor-facing one is LeadIQ, which she described as an "AI-powered lead distribution platform, focusing on matching workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitating engagement with our financial advisors." The other two, DevGen AI (developer efficiency, code modernization) and Parable (data analysis and summarization), are not described as advisor tools.
The 3Q25 10-Q (November 2025) says Wealth Management non-compensation expenses increased primarily from higher marketing and business development costs and increased technology spend.

On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), Ted Pick said the firm continues to invest in each of its three segments, including Wealth, "via human capital and technology." He said growth plans embed increasing adoption of AI tools across the enterprise and the client base.

On the same 4Q25 call (January 2026), Pick referred to "ongoing investments we're making" in AI in core technology and in AI efficiency and effectiveness tools. He expects continued operating leverage if markets are constructive and the firm executes.

On the 1Q26 call (April 2026), Pick described the firm's technology as "world-class technology, world-class cyber defense" and said it is additive to "the best trusted advisers sitting with the client." He called the adviser relationship "the key." His AI examples there were in equities and core infrastructure, not advisor tools.

The 2Q26 10-Q (August 2026) attributes the firmwide increase in non-compensation expenses of 19% for the quarter and 14% for the year-to-date period partly to increased technology spend. This is not broken out for advisors.

On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Yeshaya said the firm continues to invest across its technology stack, "embracing AI tools to support our infrastructure, business growth and people." She also said the firm's scale "supports continued investment in future technology, including AI and digital tools."

On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Pick said that if the technology is world-class, clients make decisions with their financial advisers. He said technology "can help do a lot of the early work" on clients' needs, and that the firm will keep investing "whatever it takes" to protect clients.

The 3Q26 press release (October 2026) says Wealth Management non-compensation expenses increased from a year ago primarily from higher technology spend and marketing and business development expenses.

claims.text: Schwab, 2Q25 earnings call (published July 2025): CEO Rick Wurster pointed to client activity and balance-sheet products as business fundamentals, citing margin loans up 16%, Pledged Asset Line balances at a record $21 billion, and record managed investing flows that helped assets in its wealth and asset management businesses reach all-time highs.

It said interest and dividends revenue decreased, mainly because of lower interest earned on short-term investments and government and agency obligations.

Edward Jones, 10-Q for 3Q25 (published November 2025): asset-based fee revenue rose 15% to $3,667 in the quarter, primarily from advisory program fees, on higher average market levels and continued investment of client dollars into advisory programs. Trade revenue (commissions and principal transactions) rose only 1% to $448.

Schwab, 2025 10-K (published February 2026): management says its strategy is based on the principle that trusted relationships will translate into more assets from new and existing clients, ultimately driving more revenue. It cites scale as a key competitive advantage, which lets it spread operating costs and amortize new investments over a large base of clients.

Edward Jones, 2025 10-K (published March 2026): the firm describes earning revenue on clients' assets through service fees and revenue sharing from mutual fund and insurance companies. It also earns cash solutions revenue from its Insured Bank Deposit Program, asset-based fees from trust and investment management services, and fees tied to its Money Market Fund. In Advisory Solutions, clients can elect a research model, in which the firm assumes full investment discretion, or a custom model built with their financial advisor.

Morgan Stanley, 2025 10-K (published February 2026): Wealth Management states that any revenues it earns on client assets vary depending on the services and products provided. It reports advisor-led client assets of $5,715 billion at December 31, 2025, of which fee-based client assets were $2,753 billion, or 48%.

Schwab, April 2026 monthly activity report (published May 2026): Schwab earns a fixed net yield on client margin loans and short credits tied to certain long/short strategies. It excludes those balances from average interest-earning assets starting in December 2025. It reports transactional sweep cash held on the balance sheet, including bank sweep deposits and broker-dealer cash balances.

Edward Jones, 2Q26 10-Q (published August 2026): the firm splits net revenue into fee revenue, trade revenue, net interest and dividends revenue, and other revenue. Advisory program fees are based on the average daily market value of client assets, so they move with market values and with client dollars invested or divested. Account and activity fees depend on the number of client accounts and the variety of services. Trade revenue depends on trading volume, product mix, trade size and margins earned, all of which can be affected by market volatility.

questions.text: What will receiving financial advice in the future look like for clients?

claims.text: More holistic, bespoke advice supported by technology and AI: on the 1Q26 earnings call (published April 2026), Raymond James CEO Paul Shoukry said advisers "have been expected and will continue to be expected to provide more holistic and bespoke financial advice to their clients over time." He said this requires the firm to provide technology, and that "AI can actually help." He cited $1.1 billion spent on technology and AI, covering adviser tools and client tools, plus lending (SBL and mortgage) and insurance.

Wider planning and new client segments and channels: the Edward Jones 2025 10-K (published March 2026) says the Partnership is investing in initiatives to meet clients' planning, investing, saving, spending, borrowing and comprehensive needs. These include Financial Planning Services, where clients "receive a more personalized experience with additional planning capabilities." They also include High Net Worth, Workplace, and a new digital platform for Next Generation investors. The filing says the Partnership "cannot reliably predict the timing or outcome of the initiatives."

Team-based, one-stop-shop service for wealthier households: Cerulli's Global Wealth Transfer research (published October 2025) says that in the HNW space, practices across all intermediary channels are increasingly creating team-based structures. They are also receiving enhanced home-office service and product support, "allowing advisors to be clients' one-stop shop for all their needs." Cerulli also finds a significant uptake in advice consumption and reliance on advisors as investors move into their 50s.

Earlier engagement and a defined premium experience for mass-affluent prospects: Cerulli (published March 2026) says future prospects are likely to hold several financial-services provider relationships (banking, retirement plans, insurance, mortgages, tax preparation) before reaching wealth-management minimums. Its analyst says providers will need to engage prospects earlier or find better ways to displace incumbents. He also says providers must define what a premium experience entails. Cerulli reports that 32% of affluent respondents prefer the same provider for investing and banking and have already chosen to do so. Opportunities to engage new clients fall from 44% among the affluent under 30 to 24% among those in their 50s.

Platform infrastructure that follows client choice of technology: on the 2Q26 call (published July 2026), Schwab CEO Rick Wurster said Schwab is building a technology platform to support the industry "well into the future." He said the firm is "actively building infrastructure to support client activity on the technology of clients' choice," including possible digital markets infrastructure and tokenized securities. He said it is unclear how much the tokenization market will take off. He also pointed to Schwab's combination of "people in AI" and scale.

Advice valued more under uncertainty: on the 1Q25 call (published April 2025), Morgan Stanley's CFO said clients "continue to entrust us with more of their assets, reinforcing the value they place on advice." She also said "uncertainty has increased the value of advice."

Alternatives and AI tools for advisors (trade press, indicative only): InvestmentNews (published 2026-10-14) reports that Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo continue to boost sales of alternative investments and to develop AI functions for financial advisors in 2026. It says advisors sell alternatives to clients seeking higher yields and diversification.

questions.text: Where is the industry heading on fee structures and pricing transparency?

claims.text: Position: pressure shows up as transparency and unbundling, not blanket cuts. A research piece published 2026-04-08 ("Can advisory fees survive the collapse of planning costs?", citing McKinsey) says it expects repricing of services where clients see no differentiation, such as basic tax projections. It calls the fear of an immediate industry-wide fee freefall "likely overstated". It says fee rates for relationships of more than $1 million have stayed at about 104 basis points since 2019, and that fee pressure will be uneven, "manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points."

Position: client demand for fee transparency is strong. A Wealthtender study (published 2025-08-13) reports that 73% of people consider fee transparency the most important trust factor. It also reports that 38% of survey participants identified lack of fee transparency as a red flag. Pricing was the top factor (48%) in final advisor selection, though the source says the cheapest option is not necessarily best.

Position: fees are drifting lower through passive products and mutual-fund fee changes. The Raymond James 10-K (period ended 2025-09-30, published 2025-11-25) says asset management fees may decline over time because of competition and contract renegotiation. It says the shift to passive products generates lower fees than active products, and that a continued trend toward passive investments or changes in the fee structure of asset management accounts would hurt revenues. The Edward Jones 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says clients' mutual fund holdings have been affected by industry changes in fee structures, and that the firm has seen and may continue to see decreased margins on mutual funds. Bank of America's Q1 2026 10-Q (published 2026-05-01) cites "lower AUM pricing" as a partial offset to higher investment and brokerage services income.

Position: the research view (fee rates steady, pressure uneven) and the firms' risk-factor language (fees may decline) point in different directions on overall fee levels. The research says fees above $1 million have held at about 104 bps and rejects a blanket reduction. Raymond James and Edward Jones name fee decline or margin compression as risks.

Position: firms say they will adapt pricing to competition and client preferences. On the Raymond James fiscal Q2 2026 call (period ended 2026-03-31, published 2026-04-22), the CEO said the firm wants a "profitable and competitive and fair pricing structure". He said it would be flexible and open to evolving if the industry moves based on competitive pressures and client preferences, and that it reviews pricing, fees and payout on an ongoing basis.

Position: some firms present transparency and low cost as part of their model. Schwab's Q2 2026 10-Q (published 2026-08-07) describes its strategy as offering a broad range of products "with a focus on transparency, value, and trust". It says management couples scale with expense discipline to keep costs low and products affordable. Schwab's 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) says its operating efficiency lets it price products and services competitively.

Position: distributors are adding platform charges. Trade press (published 2026-09-29) reports that Merrill's new "support fee" caps out at 10 basis points. It says Merrill's fee-based program pricing is, per sources, typically 1.00% to 1.40% and as high as 1.75%. It also says sources trace platform tolls at large distributors to the zeroing out of commissions, and that Schwab introduced data fees over seven years ago. This is trade-press reporting, not a firm disclosure.

claims.text: Edward Jones's 10-Q for the second quarter of 2026 (published 2026-08-07) states the Partnership ended the quarter with $2.6 trillion of assets under care (AUC), including $1.2 trillion of advisory programs AUC, and with 20,514 financial advisors. Both inputs are disclosed, but the filing does not state a per-advisor figure.

Raymond James's FY2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) states that total client assets under administration (AUA) in its Private Client Group segment were $1.67 trillion as of September 30, 2025, of which $1.01 trillion was fee-based AUA, with 8,943 employee and independent contractor financial advisors. The figures cover the PCG segment only, and the filing does not state a per-advisor figure.

The comparison is not like-for-like because each firm uses its own asset measure. Edward Jones reports "assets under care" (Q2 2026 10-Q). Raymond James reports PCG "assets under administration" (FY2025 10-K).

Morgan Stanley's January 2026 deck defines Total Client Assets as Wealth Management client assets plus Investment Management AUM. Its Wealth Management client assets include advisor-led brokerage, self-directed brokerage, workplace and stock plan services, and retirement plan services. It notes that some WM assets are also counted in IM's AuM. Schwab's reported total client assets, by contrast, come from a model it describes as leading in self-directed investors and RIAs. A total-assets-to-advisors ratio would therefore mix advised and non-advised assets, and the firms differ in how much of each they hold.

The measurement dates differ across the evidence. Edward Jones is as of June 2026 (10-Q published 2026-08-07). Raymond James is as of September 30, 2025 (10-K). Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management figures are as of September 30, 2026 (supplement published 2026-10-14). Schwab's are as of August 31, 2026 (monthly report published 2026-09-15). Bank of America GWIM's are as of September 30, 2026. Asset levels moved materially between these dates, so ratios built from them would not be same-date.

claims.text: Newest first. All items below come from trade press (indicative, not authoritative), not from Raymond James filings. It said Raymond James had record quarter-end client assets under administration of $1.87 trillion, up 1% sequentially and 12% year-over-year. Private Client Group net revenue was a record $3.06 billion, up 15% year-over-year, with pre-tax income of $458 million, up 10%. Domestic PCG net new assets rose 88% for the fiscal year to a record of more than $98 billion. Non-GAAP EPS was $3.59 on revenue of $4.74 billion, up 13%.

The same 2026-10-29 article says Raymond James no longer reports advisor headcount, and that it had about 8,900 advisors the last time headcount was officially broken out. These are risk-based model portfolios combining equity and fixed income with a dedicated alternatives sleeve covering private markets and hedged strategies, aimed at advisors serving high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients. Private Client Group President Tash Elwyn said the firm is "committed to being a destination for private wealth advisors and the clients they serve." The firm's asset management services group oversees portfolio construction for the models.

Also on 2026-09-29, the trade press reported that nearly 450 advisors have earned the Raymond James Private Wealth Advisor designation since it launched in 2022, per the firm. It said CEO Shoukry has emphasized building the advisory ranks through individualized recruitment rather than large-scale acquisitions. It also said the firm launched proprietary active ETFs in October 2025 and is piloting an AI-powered advisor assistant called Raimond.

On 2026-09-24, InvestmentNews reported that Raymond James Financial Services welcomed a five-advisor team, Harris Wealth Partners of Rochester, New York, from Commonwealth Financial Network, adding approximately $500 million in client assets to its independent advisor channel.

On 2026-09-16, WealthManagement.com reported, citing an SEC filing and a spokesperson, that Raymond James launched a firm-wide SIMPLE IRA Employer Advisory and Consulting Services Program, partnered with Capital Group American Funds, for small businesses with up to 100 employees. It was made available to its roughly 8,900 advisors.

On 2026-08-26, trade press reported a recruit to Raymond James Financial Services, an advisor with more than 31 years of experience, and said the firm has been particularly active attracting practices with affluent and business-owner clientele.
